name: Illusion of external agency
statement: People who talk themselves into liking a mediocre outcome can forget that they did it, and credit an insightful, powerful and benevolent outside agent instead.
meaning: The claim has two halves and only the second is unusual. The first is that people are good at making peace with outcomes they cannot change, and poor at predicting that they will. Gilbert and his colleagues call the resulting satisfaction self-generated, and treat it as the work of a psychological immune system that runs without announcing itself. The second half is the inference that follows. For an agent to hand somebody an optimal outcome on purpose, the agent must know which outcome is best, want the person to have it, and be able to arrange matters. The paper calls those three insight, benevolence and influence. Where two of them are already established, an outcome that feels optimal becomes evidence for the third. Because the satisfaction was manufactured internally, the evidence is worthless, and the inference is the illusion. Gilbert and his colleagues aim this at belief in God, and their abstract says so. Agent detection is a separate entry and a separate claim. That one is about reading purpose into ambiguous motion and sound. This one is about reading intent off an outcome whose goodness the person supplied.

origin.who: Daniel T. Gilbert, Ryan P. Brown, Elizabeth C. Pinel and Timothy D. Wilson
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: One paper of three experiments, at 79(5), 690-700. It opens on a Bertrand Russell epigram, cited as 1947/1997, pages 86 to 87, in which Russell says he cannot attribute the cruelty of history to a being who is wise, beneficent and omnipotent. The three attributes the studies test are drawn from that sentence. The authors state on page 690 that they do not deny the existence of God, and that they are arguing for a mechanism by which people may wrongly conclude that something other than themselves arranged their fate.

evidence:
Each study set up an agent already known to have two of the three attributes, then measured whether participants granted it the third. All three ran on undergraduates at the University of Texas at Austin for course credit.

Study 1 tested influence. Seventy-seven women chose a teammate by picking one of four folders, all of which in fact held the same autobiography. Control participants had rated the four candidates first; optimizing participants had not, and so had made no prior commitment about which was best. Everyone was then told that a flash of light during an earlier task had subliminally primed the symbol on the best-matched folder. Ten participants were removed for suspicion, procedural error, or having spotted which folder was which, leaving 67. Optimizing participants liked their teammate more, 6.03 against 5.70 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 65) = 7.55, p = .008. They were also readier to believe the subliminal message had steered them, 4.00 against 3.18, F(1, 65) = 4.07, p = .048.

Study 2 tested insight, and used a choice rather than a rating. Sixty-seven students, 23 men and 44 women, were told that a device called a SmartRadio had picked one of two songs for them to hear three times through. It always picked the song pretested as the worse of the pair. Optimizing participants learned that verdict before hearing the excerpts; control participants heard the excerpts first. Six were removed, leaving 61. The measure was whether participants let the same device choose again on a second trial. Six of 31 control participants did, 19%, against 13 of 30 optimizing participants, 43%, chi-square(1, 61) = 4.09, p = .042. Asked which device they would buy, 5 control participants said the chosen one, 16%, against 15 optimizing participants, 50%, chi-square(1, 61) = 7.94, p < .005.

Study 3 tested benevolence and is the smallest. Forty-nine women were assigned to be either the recipient of a gift or an observer of somebody else receiving it, and either learned which gift had been picked before rating the two options or after. The gift was always the stuffed animal, pretested as the less desirable of the pair against a voucher for a tank of petrol. Cells held 12, 13, 12 and 12 people. The headline test is a planned weighted contrast setting the optimizing recipients against the other three cells combined. On how considerate they judged the giver, that contrast gave F(1, 45) = 16.33, p < .001, with optimizing recipients at 6.58 and control recipients at 5.68. Against control recipients alone the contrast was F(1, 45) = 5.09, p = .028. Among observers, who had no stake in liking the gift, the two conditions did not differ, reported as F < 1.

replication.headline: No replication attempt of any of the three studies was found. Semantic Scholar lists 77 papers citing the original, and none of them repeats the experiments.
replication.detail:
There is a single source for this effect and nothing behind it. The three paradigms are elaborate one-offs, built around a fake subliminal prime, a fake radio and a fake gift-giver, and none of them was picked up. Searching Europe PMC for the exact phrase 'illusion of external agency' returns one record, which is the 2000 paper itself. Semantic Scholar lists 77 citing papers and OpenAlex lists 52; the titles were read in full and none announces a replication, a reproduction or a preregistered test. The citing literature reaches for the paper as a reference for affective forecasting, for the psychology of religion, and latterly for taxonomies of bias in data visualisation, rather than as a result to check.

The absence is not a verdict. Nothing here says the effect is false, and no failed attempt was found either. What the corpus records is that a claim about the psychological roots of religious belief, published in the field's flagship journal, has rested since 2000 on 67, 61 and 49 undergraduates, without anybody running it again.

limits:
The three studies are small and the samples are narrow. Every participant was a University of Texas at Austin undergraduate taking introductory psychology. Studies 1 and 3 recruited women only, for stated design reasons: same-sex partner choice in Study 1, and gifts with differing appeal by sex in Study 3. Study 3's four cells held twelve or thirteen people each. Exclusions were sizeable and were made after data collection, with 10 of 77 dropped in Study 1 and 6 of 67 in Study 2.

No standardised effect size appears in the three results sections, all of which were read in full from the scanned article. The paper reports F ratios, chi-squares and p values, with cell means and standard deviations in its three tables, so the structured effect-size fields on this page are empty rather than filled with a figure computed here. Several of the reported p values sit against the conventional threshold: .048 for the key measure in Study 1, .042 in Study 2, and .028 and .046 for the specific contrasts in Study 3. Table 1 also marks two of its rows, best teammate and confidence in winning, at p < .10, and those two were averaged into the team goodness index that the text reports at p = .05.

Study 3's headline statistic is a contrast with weights of 3 for the optimizing recipients and -1 for each other cell, chosen in advance to match the prediction. It is not an interaction term, and it is not interchangeable with one.

The search for a replication covered Europe PMC by exact phrase, PubMed, Crossref bibliographic search, the complete citing lists held by Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex, and general web search. It also covered the FORRT Replication Database, whose current FReD spreadsheet was downloaded from the project's OSF storage; the file holds no row mentioning the paper, its DOI, or the surname Pinel. Only 15 of the 77 citing records carried an abstract, so the scan of that literature rested on titles for the rest.
misreadings:
The commonest error is to report this as evidence that religious belief is a mistake. The paper says the opposite in as many words. Its coda states that human lives may or may not be guided by a wise and loving God, and that psychology experiments cannot resolve an inherently theological question. The claim on offer is that a mechanism exists which can produce the belief without the agent, which leaves the theological question exactly where it was.

The second error is to treat the three studies as three measurements of one effect. They share a logic and nothing else. Different paradigm, different agent, different dependent measure, different sample, and in Study 2 a behavioural choice rather than a rating. Three demonstrations that agree is a weaker thing than one effect measured three times, and pooling their participant counts into a single headline number overstates what was done.

A third is to read Study 1 as being about subliminal messages. No message was ever presented. The flashes of light carried nothing, and what was measured is whether participants believed a prime had worked on them.

A fourth is to confuse this with agent detection, the Barrett and Guthrie line of work on jumpy detection of agents in ambiguous motion and sound. Both reach for religion as the thing to be explained. Neither shares a paradigm, a measure or a literature with the other, and evidence about one says nothing about the other.

A fifth is to take Morewedge's 2009 paper as a follow-up, because its title, 'Negativity bias in attribution of external agency', carries the same phrase. Its abstract reports the reverse pairing: participants attributed losses and unfavourable offers to an external agent more often than wins and favourable ones, which the paper calls a negative agency bias. It asks whether bad outcomes attract agency attributions, where Gilbert and his colleagues ask what a good-feeling outcome licenses people to infer about an agent already in view. No paper was located treating either as a test of the other.

Bibliographic details verified at Crossref.
